transcript.text:
Here's a quick troubleshooting checklist, starting with the easiest fixes:

## 1. Basic checks (2 minutes)
• Power: Is the interior light on? If not, check the plug, outlet (test with another device), and circuit breaker.
• Thermostat setting: Make sure it wasn't bumped to "off" or a warm setting. Fridge should be about 37°F / 3°C, freezer 0°F / -18°C.
• Door seal: Close the door on a piece of paper. If it slides out easily, the gasket may be leaking. Also make sure nothing is stopping the door from closing fully.

## 2. Airflow problems
• Blocked vents: Food pushed against the vents inside (often at the back or between freezer and fridge) can stop cold air from circulating. Clear space around them.
• Freezer cold but fridge warm? This usually points to airflow: a blocked vent, a frosted-over evaporator coil, or a failed evaporator fan (listen for a fan running in the freezer when the door is closed and the fridge is running).

## 3. Condenser coils (very common culprit)
• Located at the back or behind the bottom front grille. Unplug the fridge and vacuum/brush off dust and pet hair.
• Make sure the fridge has a few inches of space around it for ventilation.

## 4. Listen to it
• Totally silent: Possible issue with the thermostat, control board, start relay, or compressor.
• Clicking on and off every few minutes: Often a bad start relay (a cheap, easy part to replace).
• Humming but not cooling: Could be the condenser fan (near the compressor at the back bottom) not spinning, or a compressor problem.

## 5. Defrost issue
• If you see heavy frost buildup on the back wall of the freezer, the auto-defrost system may have failed. As a temporary fix, unplug the fridge for 24 to 48 hours with the doors open (towels down!) to melt it, then plug it back in.

## When to call a technician
• Compressor not running, a refrigerant leak (oily spots, hissing), or if the fridge is old and repairs would be costly. A fridge over about 12 to 15 years old may be worth replacing instead.

Meanwhile: Keep the doors closed as much as possible. Food is generally safe for about 4 hours in a fridge without cooling. Move perishables to a cooler with ice if it'll be longer.

If you tell me what you're seeing (freezer working or not, any noises, frost, brand/age), I can help narrow it down.
freezer is fine, freezes food solid. fridge part is warm, milk going off. Samsung, about 6 yrs old. no burning smell or tripping

That pattern (freezer fine, fridge warm) on a Samsung that age very likely means ice buildup on the fridge's evaporator coil, which blocks airflow. Many Samsung models use a separate cooling system for the fridge section ("Twin Cooling"), and frosted-over fridge coils are a well-known issue.

## Step 1: Confirm it
• Listen for the fridge fan. With the fridge door closed, you should hear a fan running inside the fridge section when the unit is cooling. Press the door light switch to trick it and listen. No fan sound, or a scraping/ticking noise, suggests ice is blocking it.
• Look for frost/ice. Check the back wall of the fridge compartment and the vents. Water pooling under the crisper drawers or ice on the back panel are strong clues.
• Check vents. Make sure food isn't pressed against the vents at the back/top of the fridge.

## Step 2: Defrost it (free fix)
Option A: Manual defrost
1. Move food to coolers/freezer.
2. Unplug the fridge, leave doors open for 24 to 48 hours, towels on the floor.
3. Plug back in. The fridge should get cold within a few hours.

Option B: Forced defrost mode (faster, model-dependent)
On many Samsung models, press and hold two buttons together (often Power Freeze + Fridge, or Energy Saver + Fridge) for about 8 to 10 seconds until the display goes blank or beeps, then press a button until "Fd" appears. Leave it 20 to 30 minutes. Search your model number + "forced defrost" for the exact combo (model number is on a sticker inside the fridge door frame).

## Step 3: If it comes back
If the fridge cools after defrosting but goes warm again within days or weeks, the auto-defrost system is failing. Common causes:
• Faulty defrost heater or defrost sensor (inexpensive parts)
• Blocked defrost drain, so water refreezes
• Failing fridge evaporator fan motor

These are DIY-able if you're handy (YouTube has guides for most Samsung models), or a typical technician call. It's usually not worth replacing a 6-year-old fridge over this.

## Meanwhile
Keep perishables (milk, meat, leftovers) in a cooler with ice or in the freezer. Anything above 40°F / 4°C for more than 2 hours should be tossed.

can hear a faint scraping/ticking from the freezer sometimes. moved food off the vents, no difference, hardly any cold air from the slots at the back. thick white frost on the back of the freezer too, more than ive seen. dont know my full model no, just starts RB34

That confirms it. The scraping/ticking is almost certainly the freezer fan blades hitting ice, and the thick frost means the evaporator coil is iced over.

On the RB34 range, there's one cooling coil, located behind the back panel of the freezer. A fan blows that cold air up a duct into the fridge. When the coil and fan get iced up, the freezer stays cold (it's right next to the coil), but almost no air reaches the fridge. That's why you're getting very little from the vents.

## Fix: Full manual defrost
1. Empty both compartments. Put freezer food in cool boxes or bags, or ask a neighbour.
2. Unplug the fridge (switching off at the wall is fine).
3. Leave both doors open for 24 hours if you can. Some ice behind the back panel can take that long to melt. Put towels on the floor and in the bottom of the freezer, and change them as they soak.
4. To speed it up, put a bowl of hot water in the freezer and shut the door for 15 to 20 minutes, then repeat. A hairdryer on low can help too, but keep it moving and well away from plastic.
5. Don't chip at the ice with a knife or screwdriver. It's easy to puncture a refrigerant line, and that's usually the end of the fridge.
6. Dry it out, plug it back in, and give it a few hours before restocking. The fridge should start getting proper cold air from the vents again, and the scraping should stop.

A forced defrost mode exists on some models, but the button combo varies. For a 6-year-old frozen-solid coil, a full manual defrost is more reliable anyway.

## Find your full model number
The sticker is on the inside wall of the fridge compartment, usually low down on the side near the crisper drawers. It'll be something like RB34T6xxxxx. You'll want it if you need parts or a technician.

## Watch whether it comes back
Frost this thick usually means the automatic defrost has stopped working. If the fridge goes warm again in 1 to 3 weeks, the likely causes are:
• Defrost heater or defrost sensor failed (cheap parts, moderate DIY: remove the freezer back panel)
• Blocked or frozen defrost drain, so meltwater refreezes into a lump at the bottom of the coil
• Less often, the control board

Also check the freezer door seal. A leak lets in moist air, which builds frost fast. Look for tears, gaps, or a door that doesn't snap shut.

If you'd rather not DIY, a fridge engineer can diagnose this quickly. It's a common Samsung repair and normally well worth doing on a 6-year-old fridge.

## Food safety
Anything perishable from the fridge (milk, meat, fish, leftovers, soft cheese) that's been above 5°C for a while should be binned. If in doubt, throw it out. Freezer food that's still frozen solid is fine.
